paper_metadata.title: Accelerated quantum Monte Carlo with mitigated error on noisy quantum computer

summary: The paper proposes quantum-circuit Monte Carlo (QCMC), a gate-based hybrid algorithm for real-time many-body simulation, and shows on small examples that a first-order leading-order-rotation (LOR) formulation can reduce sign-problem variance relative to a classical-equivalent zeroth-order Pauli expansion. Numerical demonstrations use a 3-site Fermi-Hubbard model encoded into 6 qubits, a 6-spin Heisenberg model, and noisy-simulation settings such as 0.03% two-qubit gate error, 10,000–200,000 Monte Carlo samples, and variance-reduction factors up to about 4×10^6 in the best reported regime.

experiments.description: Quantum-circuit Monte Carlo (QCMC) for real-time evolution of many-body systems using exact summation formulas, with emphasis on second-order leading-order-rotation (LOR) and Pauli-operator-expansion (POE) circuits, including error-mitigated evaluation of transition amplitudes.

algorithm.variant: Quantum-circuit Monte Carlo (QCMC) with exact summation formulas; second-order POE and LOR variants; compact and forward-backward circuits; probabilistic error cancellation and postselection-based error mitigation

hyperparameters.num_shots_Ms: 1 for optimal unbiased estimator without postselection; larger Ms used with postselection
hyperparameters.formula_order: 0th, 1st, 2nd, and higher-order discussed; experiments focus on 0th-order POE and 1st-order LOR, plus 2nd-order error-mitigation analysis
hyperparameters.Hamiltonian_decomposition: H = sum_j h_j sigma_j with Pauli terms
hyperparameters.controlled_correction_gate_error_rate_et: considered as eta * epsilon in analysis; examples eta = 0.1 and eta = 1 in Fig. 7
hyperparameters.evolution_time_t: varied in figures; examples up to t = 4
hyperparameters.system_size_examples: Fermi-Hubbard model on 3 sites (6 qubits) and Heisenberg model on 6 spins

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Hamiltonian terms are expressed as sums of Pauli operators; the algorithm samples random unitary correction operators and evaluates transition amplitudes between specified initial and final states
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate transition amplitudes of the form <psi_f|e^{iHt*} O e^{-iHt}|psi_i> and observables <psi_i|e^{iHt} O e^{-iHt}|psi_i> using Monte Carlo with quantum subroutines
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Error mitigation via probabilistic error cancellation and/or postselection in forward-backward circuits; no QUBO/Ising optimization constraints
problem_formulation.problem_hamiltonian: H = sum_j h_j sigma_j; examples include Fermi-Hubbard and Heisenberg Hamiltonians mapped to qubits

problem_instance.description: Real-time simulation of quantum many-body dynamics; numerical demonstrations on the 1D Fermi-Hubbard model and the Heisenberg model

dataset_specification.description: Fermi-Hubbard model on 3 sites (6 qubits) with initial state c†_{1,↑} c†_{2,↓} c†_{3,↑}|Vac>; Heisenberg model on 6 spins with initial state |010101>

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Jordan-Wigner transformation used to encode the Fermi-Hubbard model into qubits; Pauli-term expansion and sampling distribution based on |c(s)|
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Numerical simulation on a classical computer of the quantum circuits/noise model; figures compare exact, raw, postselected, purified, and Trotter results; Monte Carlo sample sizes reported per experiment

noise_model.error_mitigation_method: probabilistic error cancellation; forward-backward circuit; postselection; tomography purification

noise_parameters.gate_error_rate: p = 0.03% per controlled-NOT gate in the numerical demonstration

noise_model.mitigation_details: Pauli error model with p_sigma = p/15 for two-qubit gates; quasi-probability decomposition; postselection on |0>^n in forward-backward circuit; tomography purification of ancillary qubit
noise_model.classical_solver: classical Monte Carlo / classical simulation of noisy circuits for numerical demonstrations
noise_model.classical_preprocessing: Jordan-Wigner mapping for Fermi-Hubbard; construction of sampling distribution P(s) proportional to product of coefficient magnitudes
noise_model.classical_postprocessing: Monte Carlo averaging of measured binary outcomes; phase correction via theta_s; postselection-based reconstruction using <X_a>, <Y_a>, <Z_a>

classical_baselines.method_name: classical monte carlo / green's function monte carlo
classical_baselines.unit: exponential in evolution time and Hamiltonian scale

classical_baselines.method_name: classical monte carlo / green's function monte carlo

speedup_claims.factor: polynomial on a fault-tolerant quantum computer
speedup_claims.baseline_method: classical QMC / Green's function Monte Carlo in the sign-problem regime
speedup_claims.conditions: fault-tolerant hardware; exact summation formulas; suppressing gate error to arbitrarily small values with quantum error correction
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper argues polynomial scaling in the fault-tolerance limit, but does not demonstrate it on hardware.

speedup_claims.factor: variance reduced by several orders of magnitude
speedup_claims.conditions: noisy quantum computer; second-order LOR formula; example h_tot t = 4 and gate error rate 0.1
speedup_claims.caveats: Claim is based on analytical variance estimates and numerical examples, not a real QPU experiment.
This is a sample-size reduction factor inferred from the variance comparison.

speedup_claims.conditions: second-order LOR formula; fitted from numerical results; small error rate regime
speedup_claims.caveats: This is a fitted scaling law for the minimum rate of increase of variance, not a direct runtime speedup.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: Polynomial on a fault-tolerant quantum computer; on noisy hardware, variance scales approximately as exp(4 gamma h_tot t) with gamma depending on error rate and time step
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: Classical QMC / Green's function Monte Carlo suffers exponential variance in the sign-problem regime, approximately exp(4 h_tot t) for the zeroth-order classical-equivalent case

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: A noisy gate-based quantum computer with low two-qubit error rates and enough qubits to run shallow QCMC circuits; the paper’s numerical study uses a classical simulator rather than a QPU.
limiting_factors: No real quantum hardware benchmark is reported
The main comparison is against classical Monte Carlo / Trotter baselines
The demonstrated systems are small (6 qubits / 3 sites / 6 spins)
Performance depends strongly on sampling variance and error mitigation overhead
No practical crossover size is established

notes: The paper reports numerical demonstrations on a classical simulator (QuESTlink) rather than a real QPU.

The 6-qubit count is inferred from the explicitly stated Fermi-Hubbard encoding into 2N_L qubits with N_L = 3; the Heisenberg example uses 6 spins but the paper does not separately state a qubit count for that circuit.
Circuit depth is described analytically (proportional to N; forward-backward doubles depth) rather than as a single numeric depth value.
The paper is gate-based and not an annealing study.
The paper presents a theoretical algorithm and noisy-simulation demonstrations, not a hardware advantage benchmark.
It reports variance reduction and mitigation behavior, but not a demonstrated end-to-end quantum advantage on a QPU.

experiments.description: Numerical demonstration of the forward-backward circuit with postselection and tomography purification for the 1D Fermi-Hubbard model, showing error mitigation on a 6-qubit encoding.

algorithm.variant: Forward-backward circuit with postselection and tomography purification applied to QCMC / first-order summation formula

key_results: The paper reports that postselection and tomography purification significantly suppress the error in the observable evolution compared with raw noisy results.
The numerical example uses a 3-site Fermi-Hubbard model encoded into 6 qubits.
